scenes.tts: A mouse licks sugar water and keeps licking. What has its brain just worked out?
scenes.visual: Title card: Which Taste, and How Good? Then a mouse at a lick spout; a lick counter in the corner ticks upward.
scenes.narration: A mouse licks sugar water and keeps licking. What has its brain just worked out?

scenes.tts: Two questions hide in that licking. Which taste does its brain register? And how much does the mouse want it?
scenes.visual: Two thought bubbles over the mouse, each with a question mark: one holds a blank taste label, the other an arrow pointing toward the spout.
scenes.narration: Two questions hide in that licking. Which taste does its brain register? And how much does the mouse want it?

scenes.tts: Are those one signal or two? And where can they be pulled apart?
scenes.visual: Question on screen: one signal or two? Where can they be pulled apart?
scenes.narration: Are those one signal or two? And where can they be pulled apart?

scenes.tts: Call the first one identity: which taste it is.
scenes.visual: The label bubble becomes a card titled Identity, listing sweet, bitter, sour, salty, umami.
scenes.narration: Call the first one identity: which taste it is.

scenes.tts: Call the second one value: whether the animal is drawn to it or turns away, and how strongly. Its good-or-bad sign is called valence.
scenes.visual: The arrow bubble becomes a card titled Value: attraction or aversion, and how strong. Underneath, smaller: valence, appetitive or aversive (the sign).
scenes.narration: Call the second one value: whether the animal is drawn to it or turns away, and how strongly. Its good-or-bad sign is called valence.

scenes.tts: Taste cells are not neurons. They must hand their news to a fibre.
scenes.visual: Cut-away of a taste bud: elongated taste cells with a nerve fibre ending at their base. Label: taste cells are not neurons.
scenes.narration: Taste cells are not neurons. They must hand their news to a fibre.

scenes.tts: In mice, type two cells include populations that respond mainly to sweet, to bitter or to umami. Some cells respond to more than one.
scenes.caption: In mice, type II cells include populations that respond mainly to sweet, to bitter or to umami. Some cells respond to more than one.
scenes.visual: Representative type II cells highlighted in colour inside the bud, each tinted for the quality it responds to mainly: sweet, bitter, umami; one cell carries both the sweet and umami tints. Label: mouse; schematic of predominant selectivity, with some overlap.
scenes.narration: In mice, type II cells include populations that respond mainly to sweet, to bitter or to umami. Some cells respond to more than one.

scenes.tts: Type three cells sense acid. They make conventional synapses onto the fibre.
scenes.caption: Type III cells sense acid. They make conventional synapses onto the fibre.
scenes.visual: A third cell, labelled type III, tagged sour, with a cluster of vesicles at its base facing the fibre.
scenes.narration: Type III cells sense acid. They make conventional synapses onto the fibre.

scenes.tts: Type two cells have no conventional vesicular synapse. They release A T P through a channel.
scenes.caption: Type II cells have no conventional vesicular synapse. They release ATP through a channel.
scenes.visual: Zoom on a type II cell's base: no synaptic vesicles; small ATP dots leave through a channel patch toward the fibre. On-screen labels: CALHM1/3; no conventional vesicular synapse.
scenes.narration: Type II cells have no conventional vesicular synapse. They release ATP through a channel.

scenes.tts: On its own, the main channel subunit opens slowly in cultured cells. Its time constant is over half a second.
scenes.visual: A slowly rising gate-opening curve. Labels: CALHM1 alone; time constant above 500 ms; cultured cells; illustrative curve.
scenes.narration: On its own, the main channel subunit opens slowly in cultured cells. Its time constant is over half a second.

scenes.tts: A type two cell's spike is brief. Can a gate that slow keep up?
scenes.caption: A type II cell's spike is brief. Can a gate that slow keep up?
scenes.visual: A brief spike drawn under the slow curve; the curve has barely risen when the spike ends. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: A type II cell's spike is brief. Can a gate that slow keep up?

scenes.tts: Barely. Adding a partner subunit speeds opening to about ten milliseconds. These are cultured-cell times, not delays in a living mouse.
scenes.visual: A second, fast curve rises within the spike. Labels: CALHM1 with CALHM3, about 10 ms; cultured cells; illustrative curves.
scenes.narration: Barely. Adding a partner subunit speeds opening to about ten milliseconds. These are cultured-cell times, not delays in a living mouse.

scenes.tts: And in mice lacking that partner, taste buds released no A T P in response to tastes.
scenes.caption: And in mice lacking that partner, taste buds released no ATP in response to tastes.
scenes.visual: A taste bud from a mouse lacking CALHM3: no ATP dots leave. Label: Calhm3 deleted, taste-evoked ATP release abolished.
scenes.narration: And in mice lacking that partner, taste buds released no ATP in response to tastes.

scenes.tts: Fibres from the front of the tongue have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion.
scenes.visual: The pathway begins to draw: tongue, then a line to a small cluster labelled geniculate ganglion.
scenes.narration: Fibres from the front of the tongue have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion.

scenes.tts: In rodents, signals then climb through brainstem relays and the thalamus to taste cortex, and on to the amygdala.
scenes.visual: The line extends station by station: solitary nucleus and parabrachial nucleus (brainstem), gustatory thalamus, insular cortex, then to the amygdala. Side branches leave the parabrachial nucleus for the amygdala and hypothalamus, so the drawing is a branching pathway, not a single line. Label: rodents.
scenes.narration: In rodents, signals then climb through brainstem relays and the thalamus to taste cortex, and on to the amygdala.

scenes.tts: The experiments here sample three stations: the ganglion, the cortex and the amygdala.
scenes.visual: Three stations light up: geniculate ganglion, insular cortex, amygdala. The relays between them dim. Label: relays not tested here.
scenes.narration: The experiments here sample three stations: the ganglion, the cortex and the amygdala.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. In the mouse, identity begins with which taste-cell population is driven.
scenes.visual: Callout box: The one idea. The sweet cells light up, and a fibre leaving them lights in the same colour.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. In the mouse, identity begins with which taste-cell population is driven.

scenes.tts: Many fibres pass that on selectively at low strength, and more broadly at high strength. Not all of them broaden.
scenes.visual: Two small panels of recorded response profiles: at low strength, one bar per neuron; at high strength, most neurons gain a second bar and a few do not. Label: observed pattern, mouse.
scenes.narration: Many fibres pass that on selectively at low strength, and more broadly at high strength. Not all of them broaden.

scenes.tts: Drive the sweet field of taste cortex, and a mouse is drawn in. Block that field, and trained mice struggle to recognize sweet.
scenes.visual: Cortex: the sweet field glows. Two measured-readout cards appear beside it, side by side: Recognition (trained task) and Attraction (licking); the mouse steps toward the spout. Label: mouse assays.
scenes.narration: Drive the sweet field of taste cortex, and a mouse is drawn in. Block that field, and trained mice struggle to recognize sweet.

scenes.tts: Drive the bitter field, and it turns away.
scenes.visual: The bitter field glows instead; the mouse turns away.
scenes.narration: Drive the bitter field, and it turns away.

scenes.tts: Then one manipulation pulled those two readouts apart.
scenes.visual: The two readout cards, Recognition and Attraction, slide slightly apart under the sweet field; the amygdala on the branching diagram is outlined, about to be silenced.
scenes.narration: Then one manipulation pulled those two readouts apart.

scenes.tts: Silence the amygdala, and mice still recognize sweet. But driving sweet cortex no longer draws them in.
scenes.visual: The label stays lit, and the arrow fades. Caption: recognized, but no longer drawn in. Label: mouse assays.
scenes.narration: Silence the amygdala, and mice still recognize sweet. But driving sweet cortex no longer draws them in.

scenes.tts: And the pull changes with what the body needs.
scenes.visual: The arrow grows longer beside a body-state gauge that moves toward need.
scenes.narration: And the pull changes with what the body needs.

scenes.tts: The experiments here are in mice. None of this is a human map.
scenes.visual: Scope card: mouse experiments; not a human map.
scenes.narration: The experiments here are in mice. None of this is a human map.

scenes.tts: Which taste, and how good: one cortical field bears on both, and silencing the amygdala separates them in these mouse assays.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: two measured readouts, Recognition and Attraction. With the amygdala silenced, Recognition stays lit and Attraction fades. Small branching pathway diagram beside it. Label: behavioural dissociation, mouse assays.
scenes.narration: Which taste, and how good: one cortical field bears on both, and silencing the amygdala separates them in these mouse assays.
